target_customer: Families and close friend groups who want a private shared space instead of public social networks
problem: Public social networks and noisy group chats are poor places for close circles to stay connected.

competitors.name: Path
competitors.what: Private social network for close friends
competitors.traction_then: Used by TechCrunch as the comparison point

competitors.name: Group chats (iMessage and others)
competitors.what: Existing messaging threads named as the biggest competitor

technical_complexity.rationale: A private group feed on iOS with shared content and tools is standard consumer app engineering.

defensibility.rationale: Network effects were limited to small closed groups and group chats were free substitutes; Facebook-owned Instagram launched Threads for close friends the same month (Axios, Nov 2019).

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Instagram launched a close-friends app, Threads, in late 2019; Cocoon's team joined Substack in August 2021 while the app stayed independent.

market_need_then: Not strongly evidenced; Axios and TechCrunch in Nov 2019 described a trend of small social networks, and the founders saw a gap between public networks and chat.

branding.domain_note: No domain information found; the YC site field was empty.

identity.voice_and_tone: Warm, family-oriented positioning (Lerer Hippeau post title: a shared digital space helping far-flung families stay close)

branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch and Axios at launch in Nov 2019; no evidence of merch or fan community.

brand_strength.rationale: Evocative name that suits a private nest but shared with many unrelated companies; limited evidence of brand pull.

outcome_analysis: Cocoon raised a 3 million dollar seed in 2019 and launched an iOS app for private groups in November 2019 against free group chats and Facebook-backed close-friends products. In August 2021 Substack hired the design and engineering team while the app itself was not included and was to remain independent, which is a team acqui-hire rather than a product exit. The company did not state why it stopped growing the app.
notes: No company website listed on YC and no live site found, so the site is treated as dead or unknown. TechCrunch calls Monga CEO and Cornell co-founder. Founding year not found. A Dealroom page says the app folded into Substack; Substack's own post says the app stayed independent. Education not found for either founder.
